summary:
ASTRA 2.0 is an offline astronaut health self-monitoring prototype for long-duration missions, where communication delays can limit access to ground support. It replays a 90-day simulated mission for four fictional crew members, bringing vital signs, sleep, self-reports, and cabin conditions into one dashboard. ASTRA compares recent readings with each crew member’s own baseline and shows the observations behind each finding. NASA research informed the choice of measurements and the simulation design.
Our experimental face and speech modules explore how changes in facial movement, speaking rate, and pauses might complement psychological well-being check-ins. With opt-in webcam and microphone capture, ASTRA compares these features with each participant’s own baseline. The modules show changes over time with possible expansion in Health Monitoring. Synthetic examples let users try both modules without recording themselves.
An optional Qwen3 4B companion runs locally through Ollama and offers conversation, quizzes, and text games during periods of isolation or limited connectivity. It has no access to health records and operates separately from monitoring. Together, these features explore how crews could review health trends, support regular well-being check-ins, and access recreational tools onboard.
details:
Mission replay and personal health monitoring. ASTRA starts at the end of Day 45 of a fictional 90-day mission. Users can advance one event or one day at a time and see how new observations change the dashboard. For supported measurements, ASTRA builds a personal baseline from the first 45 days using medians and median absolute deviation. Each finding shows the readings behind it, helping users distinguish a sustained change from a single unusual measurement. NASA research informed the selection of measurements and the design of the synthetic dataset.

Facial and speech analysis. The facial prototype uses MediaPipe and LibreFace to extract facial muscle movement features from webcam samples. The speech prototype uses tools including openSMILE, Silero VAD, and Meta XLS-R to analyze short microphone samples. Both modules calibrate on the participant’s own usable samples and plot feature changes over time. Users can try synthetic examples without hardware or opt into local capture with a webcam and microphone. Saved calibration contains fitted statistics, and raw recordings are excluded from the saved profile. The modules show experimental changes in observable features. They do not infer emotion, stress, or illness.

Local Qwen companion. ASTRA runs Qwen3 4B locally through Ollama as an optional recreational assistant. Crew members can chat, play text games, or request a quiz. The companion receives the conversation supplied by the user and has no access to health records, cabin readings, or replay controls.

Technology and intended impact. We built the console with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts, with a Python, FastAPI, and SQLite backend. The core runs offline after installation. The prototype demonstrates how a crew could review personal trends and their supporting evidence when ground support is delayed, while keeping experimental sensing and recreational chat separate from the health findings. The system uses synthetic mission data and has no clinical or flight validation.

Use of Super Intelligence: Accelerate Coding, Debugging, or Troubleshooting; Writing, documentation; Helps with creating audio
